periods.analysis: Harborview opened the school year with a Teacher Vacancy Rate of 3.6%, above our <=2% target and therefore appropriately yellow, even as Per-Pupil Expenditure stood at $12951, comfortably above the >=$12500 standard. The vacancy pressure was concentrated in secondary math, special education, and bilingual elementary classrooms, with the South Harbor and Airport East feeder patterns carrying the heaviest substitute load. I am encouraged that the budget picture is green, but dollars only become student outcomes when they are attached to capable adults in classrooms every morning. Our watch-item is the number of unfilled core-course sections still being covered by long-term substitutes after the tenth instructional day.
periods.recommendations: Keep the Q3 hiring command center active through October, with HR, principals, and licensure staff reviewing South Harbor, Airport East, and Bayside Middle vacancies twice weekly. Use the green $12951 per-pupil position to sustain signing stipends for hard-to-staff certifications and extend the Harborview Teacher Residency cohort by reserving spring placement slots now. Require each school with more than two vacancies to submit a coverage plan that protects intervention blocks and limits long-term substitute assignments in tested subjects.

periods.analysis: By year-end, the Teacher Vacancy Rate improved from 3.6% to 2.9%, a meaningful 0.7 percentage-point quarter-over-quarter reduction, though still above the <=2% target and still yellow. Per-Pupil Expenditure moved from $12951 to $12895, down $56 but still green and above the >=$12500 benchmark. The midyear hiring fair at Harborview Convention Center and the fast-track transcript reviews with Coastal State University helped close several elementary and special education positions. The watch-item now shifts from volume alone to retention of November and December hires through the spring testing window.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the new-hire onboarding clinics that paired novice teachers with master teachers at Lincoln, Seaport, and Northgate campuses, and make attendance mandatory for every hire made after October 1. Extend targeted recruitment into January by offering early contracts to student teachers in math, special education, and multilingual education before neighboring districts move. Finance and HR should jointly monitor whether the $12895 per-pupil level is reaching vacancy-sensitive schools through substitute reduction, planning-time protection, and mentor stipends.

periods.analysis: In 2025-Q1, the Teacher Vacancy Rate edged down from 2.9% to 2.8%, a modest 0.1 percentage-point improvement, but it remains yellow against the <=2% target. Per-Pupil Expenditure declined from $12895 to $12707, down $188 quarter over quarter, yet remains green above the >=$12500 target. The rate of improvement slowed after winter break, which tells me the easy fills are behind us and the remaining gaps are in specialized credentials and high-need campuses. Our watch-item is spring resignation intent, particularly among first- and second-year teachers in schools with elevated chronic absenteeism.
periods.recommendations: Launch a March retention pulse survey for all probationary teachers and require principal follow-up within ten school days where workload, student behavior, or planning time are flagged. Sustain the green spending posture at $12707 by protecting mentor release time and avoiding across-the-board cuts that would weaken induction. Extend the Grow Harborview paraprofessional-to-teacher pathway by adding a weekend Praxis preparation vendor and tuition support for the summer bilingual endorsement course.

periods.analysis: The quarter brought a setback: Teacher Vacancy Rate rose from 2.8% to 3.3%, a 0.5 percentage-point increase and still yellow versus the <=2% target. At the same time, Per-Pupil Expenditure rose from $12707 to $12980, up $273 and green, giving us room to act but not permission to be casual. The increase reflects early retirements, family relocations in a tight housing market, and several late spring departures from special education teams serving the Portside and West Channel clusters. The watch-item is summer pipeline conversion—how many signed letters of intent become teachers physically present at pre-service week.
periods.recommendations: Stand up a summer vacancy war room by June 15, with daily tracking of every opening by certification, campus, and candidate stage. Use the green $12980 per-pupil capacity to extend relocation support for hard-to-staff hires, especially candidates priced out of Harborview’s rental market. Lock in contracts with Coastal State University and the Bay Teachers Collaborative for a defined number of special education, math, and bilingual residents, and report conversion weekly to the superintendent’s cabinet.

periods.analysis: As the new school year opened, Teacher Vacancy Rate rose again from 3.3% to 3.4%, a 0.1 percentage-point increase that keeps the objective yellow and uncomfortably above the <=2% target. Per-Pupil Expenditure moved from $12980 to $12833, down $147, but remains green above the >=$12500 threshold. The small rise masks a harder operational reality: vacancies were narrower in elementary grades but more disruptive in high school science, special education case management, and English learner services along the Route 14 corridor. Our watch-item is whether substitute coverage begins to erode attendance interventions and ninth-grade on-track supports.
periods.recommendations: Prioritize remaining vacancies using a student-impact index, filling special education, EL, and Algebra I sections before lower-impact elective gaps. Sustain the green $12833 per-pupil investment by maintaining instructional coach coverage and extending the Residency Plus classroom co-teaching model into West Channel High and Mariner Middle. Authorize HR to issue same-week conditional offers for fully credentialed shortage-area candidates, with final background and licensure checks completed through the district’s standard safeguards.

periods.analysis: The system regained ground in 2025-Q4, with Teacher Vacancy Rate falling from 3.4% to 2.8%, a 0.6 percentage-point improvement, though still yellow against the <=2% target. Per-Pupil Expenditure increased from $12833 to $12903, up $70 and green above the >=$12500 target. The improvement followed the October educator returnship campaign, principal-led stay interviews, and better coordination between HR and the payroll team on start-date clearance. The watch-item is sustainability: we cannot let a strong hiring quarter disguise continued fragility in special education and bilingual staffing.
periods.recommendations: Make the returnship campaign permanent by keeping a quarterly list of retirees, career changers, and former Harborview teachers eligible for re-entry in shortage areas. Sustain the green $12903 per-pupil level by extending mentor stipends through the full year rather than ending support after onboarding. Require campuses that improved vacancy counts to document which practices worked—interview scheduling, candidate communication, induction routines—and replicate them in schools still above the district average.

periods.analysis: Teacher Vacancy Rate held steady at 2.8% from 2025-Q4 to 2026-Q1, which is stability but not yet success because the measure remains yellow above the <=2% target. Per-Pupil Expenditure increased from $12903 to $12919, up $16 and still green above the >=$12500 benchmark. I read the flat vacancy rate as a sign that our retention work is preventing slippage, but our pipeline is not yet strong enough to break through the 2% line. The watch-item is the April transfer and resignation window, when internal movement can create avoidable churn at high-need campuses.
periods.recommendations: Freeze nonessential midyear transfers out of schools with persistent vacancies unless there is a principal-approved coverage plan and a confirmed replacement. Sustain the green $12919 per-pupil position by continuing paid planning communities for novice teachers and extending behavioral support teams to the campuses with the highest early-career turnover risk. Begin issuing 2026-2027 early contracts in March for student teachers who meet performance benchmarks in Harborview classrooms.

periods.analysis: In 2026-Q2, Teacher Vacancy Rate increased from 2.8% to 3.2%, a 0.4 percentage-point rise that keeps the objective yellow and reminds us how quickly spring staffing can soften. Per-Pupil Expenditure increased from $12919 to $13029, up $110 and green above the >=$12500 target, the strongest funding position in this sequence. The vacancy rise is tied to end-of-year retirements, regional competition for STEM teachers, and housing-cost pressure on early-career educators near the airport and seaport employment centers. The watch-item for the next quarter is opening-day readiness: every campus needs a named teacher, resident, or qualified long-term substitute attached to every roster before families receive schedules.
periods.recommendations: Use the green $13029 per-pupil capacity to fund a focused summer retention and recruitment package: shortage-area stipends, relocation assistance, and guaranteed mentor release time for new hires. Extend partnerships with Harborview Housing, Coastal State University, and the Bay Teachers Collaborative to secure workforce housing referrals and produce more local candidates in special education, STEM, and bilingual education. By July 31, require a campus-by-campus staffing readiness review that identifies vacancies, candidate status, substitute contingencies, and principal escalation needs.

periods.analysis: Vacancies improved from 3.2% to 2.9%, but have not reached the 2% target. Per-pupil expenditure remains above its standard at $13,050. Funding capacity is favorable; filling shortage-area classrooms remains unfinished.
periods.recommendations: Maintain targeted recruitment and onboarding reviews, and verify school-level staffing coverage before treating the expenditure result as a workforce outcome.
